Juvenile Scud (Jassa falcata) emerge from the brood pouch at a total body length of approximately 0.18 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.18 centimeters], a size that facilitates early mobility within complex fouling communities. Newly released individuals possess a wet weight of about 0.00012 g [Wwb = about 0.00012 g]rams, a value derived from comparative measurements on the congener Jassa slatteryi, reflecting the diminutive starting mass characteristic of this tube-dwelling amphipod. Embryonic development is highly sensitive to thermal conditions; at a stable temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the interval between egg deposition and juvenile release averages 16.0 d [ab = 16.0 d]ays, a protracted incubation period that slows population turnover. In contrast, when reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at birth is substantially shortened to 8.8 d [ab = 8.8 d]ays, illustrating a pronounced acceleration of ontogeny under moderate warming. At the upper experimental extreme of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the incubation period lengthens slightly to 10.0 d [ab = 10.0 d]ays, a non-linear response that may reflect suboptimal thermal stress or increased metabolic demands on the brooding female.

Sexual maturation in this species is tightly coupled to both body size and environmental temperature, with marked consequences for population demography. Under cool conditions maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], puberty, defined here as the onset of functional gonadal activity, occurs at approximately 142 days after birth (142.0 d) [tp = 142.0 d], a lengthy juvenile phase that delays recruitment into the breeding population. At a warmer regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at puberty is reduced to 110 days (110.0 d) [tp = 110.0 d], reflecting faster somatic growth and earlier gametogenesis. The most rapid maturation is observed at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], where individuals reach puberty in just 69.0 d [tp = 69.0 d]ays, a nearly twofold acceleration relative to the 10 °C treatment. The body length at which this developmental milestone is attained is 0.67 centimeters [Lp = 0.67 centimeters], a measurement that appears relatively invariant across tested thermal regimes, suggesting a fixed size threshold triggers reproductive development regardless of the time required to reach it.

Adult females of Jassa falcata reach an ultimate body length of 0.82 centimeters [Li = 0.82 centimeters], which represents the maximum size attained under favorable conditions. Males, in contrast, grow to a slightly larger final length of 0.89 centimeters [Li = 0.89 centimeters], a pattern of sexual dimorphism in body size that is common among tube-building amphipods. The ultimate dry weight of individuals, calculated from length-weight regressions developed for the related species Corophium volutator, is 0.0046 g rams, a modest mass that underscores the species’ small adult body plan. These maximum sizes are typically achieved after the completion of the pubertal molt and are maintained through continued, if slowed, somatic growth during the reproductive phase. The slight but consistent size advantage in males may confer benefits in male-male competition for access to receptive females within the tube matrix, while the smaller female size is likely linked to the energetic demands of repeated brooding cycles.

Lifetime reproductive output in this amphipod varies markedly as a function of thermal environment, with cascading effects on per-capita contribution to the next generation. At a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], females produce an average of 39.0 offspring  across their entire lifespan, a relatively high fecundity achieved through slow, sustained reproductive effort over an extended adult period. When the temperature is raised to 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the lifetime number of offspring declines to 30.0 (30.0 #) , a reduction that likely reflects the trade-off between faster brood production and a compressed reproductive window. At the highest tested temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], total fecundity drops further to just 23.0 offspring , indicating that while individual broods may develop more quickly at warmer temperatures, the overall duration of reproductive activity is curtailed. These data demonstrate that the thermal optimum for lifetime reproductive output is at the cooler end of the range examined.

Longevity in Jassa falcata is profoundly influenced by temperature, shaping the organism’s overall life history strategy. At 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the lifespan extends to a maximum of 252.0 d [am = 252.0 d]ays, a duration that allows ample time for multiple broods and contributes to the elevated lifetime fecundity observed at this temperature. As temperature increases to 15 °C [T = 15 °C], maximum longevity contracts to 173.0 d [am = 173.0 d]ays, representing a reduction of over 30 percent relative to the coolest regime. At the warmest condition tested, 20 °C [T = 20 °C], individuals live no longer than 153.0 d [am = 153.0 d]ays, the shortest lifespan recorded across the experimental treatments. The inverse relationship between temperature and lifespan is consistent with classic metabolic theories of aging, wherein higher metabolic rates accelerate the accumulation of physiological wear. Despite the shorter life at high temperature, the rapid pace of maturation and brood production still permits successful reproduction, though with diminished total output compared to cooler environments.
